paras: The lynching of Robert Bryan took place on the evening of July 6, 1888, on the outskirts of Henderson, Kentucky, when about fifty masked men took the Black youth of about sixteen from the men conveying him to jail and hanged him to a tree. Bryan had been accused of stabbing to death Riley Hancock, a nineteen-year-old white man, near Smith's Mills earlier that day. A Nashville American dispatch carried the story to papers across the country, and the Hopkinsville South Kentuckian treated it as the latest in a run of mob actions at Henderson.

According to the South Kentuckian, Hancock and Bryan were riding together in a wagon near Smith's Mills in Henderson County about noon on Friday when they quarreled and came to blows. Both fell from the wagon, and in the struggle Bryan was said to have stabbed Hancock in the heart with a physician's knife with a blade of about four inches, killing him at once. The same paper noted that Hancock was a cousin of Jeff Hancock, who it said had been "murdered by a negro several weeks ago near the scene of the present lynching."

Bryan was arrested and, after an examining trial, was started toward the jail at Henderson under guard. The wire dispatch said three men set out with him, while the South Kentuckian described a party of two guards and the prisoner. About dark, when the party was within five minutes of the city, it was overtaken by a mob of fifty masked men, mounted according to the local account.
The guards were driven off "covered by a score or more of revolvers," and Bryan was snatched from them. He was taken to a nearby tree, hanged and "left dangling in mid-air."

No report of an inquest, of arrests among the masked men or of any grand jury action appears in the coverage. Kentucky weeklies were still reprinting the brief wire paragraph a week later, placing the killing "near Smith's mills, Henderson County" without further detail.

The first reports were a special to the Nashville American from Henderson, sent out under Nashville datelines of July 6 and 7 and printed on July 7 and 8 in Washington, Salt Lake City, Los Angeles, Richmond, New York, Savannah and Seattle. Headlines varied: the Evening Star used "A Boy Murderer Lynched," the Salt Lake Herald "Judge Lynch," and the Savannah Morning News "Lynched in a City. Masked Men Suspend a Black Murderer from a Tree." The Richmond Dispatch, following the Nashville dateline, headed the story "A Tennessee Lynching."

The New-York Tribune put the dispatch under the headline "Of course, the negro was lynched," presenting the outcome as expected even as its text, like every version, called Bryan "the murderer." In Maysville, Kentucky, the Evening Bulletin reduced the case to a flippant line, saying the mob "objected to his summary manner of carving the life out of Riley Hancock." Shorter versions in New England papers said only that Bryan had been arrested and then "taken by a mob and lynched."

The fullest account came from the Hopkinsville South Kentuckian on July 10, under the heading "Another Henderson Mob," which described the wagon quarrel, the knife and the examining trial and spoke of "the terrified negro." Telegram columns in Kentucky, Tennessee and Mississippi weeklies dropped Bryan's race while keeping Hancock's as "white." Later copies garbled the names, printing "Robert Bryant," "Robert Ryan" and "Ellery Hancock," and one made Hancock sixteen; the story was still circulating in South Carolina on July 25.

The accounts differ on small points: the wire put the escort at three men and the local paper at two guards, and the Savannah version had the mob overtake the party "in the town" rather than on its outskirts. Because the South Kentuckian wrote from the region and gave the most detail, its version of the escort and the place, just outside Henderson, is likely the better evidence.

bases: Fifty masked men took Robert Bryan, a Black youth accused of killing a white man, from the men conveying him to the Henderson jail and hanged him to a tree (A2, A14).
A mob given as fifty masked men seized Bryan from his guards and hanged him without trial, in retribution for the stabbing of Riley Hancock (A2, A14, A10).

The Nashville American's Henderson special carried by wire (A2, A3, A7) and the separate, more detailed account in the Hopkinsville South Kentuckian (A14) agree on the stabbing, the seizure by about fifty masked men and the hanging.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the wire text under headings such as 'A Boy Murderer Lynched' and 'Judge Lynch.', calling Bryan 'the murderer'.
The New-York Tribune headed the wire 'Of course, the negro was lynched.', treating the outcome as predictable while the text still called Bryan 'the murderer'.
The Savannah Morning News headlined 'Lynched in a City. Masked Men Suspend a Black Murderer from a Tree.'
The Maysville Evening Bulletin gave a flippant paragraph saying the mob 'objected to his summary manner of carving the life out of' Hancock.
The South Kentuckian headed its local account 'Another Henderson Mob.' and tied the killing to an earlier murder of Hancock's cousin by a Black man.

record_check.dossier: The stabbing was near Smith's Mills; the lynching was on the outskirts of Henderson, within five minutes of the city.
Seizure from guards and hanging; no pursuit of a fugitive is reported (the mob overtook the party conveying him to jail).
Papers call the perpetrators a 'mob' of about fifty masked (mounted) men; no organized band is named.
The one white death (Riley Hancock) was the precipitating stabbing attributed to Bryan, not mob violence; the mob killed one person.
Wire says three men; the local paper says two guards and reports an arrest and examining trial before the transfer.
